description:
Scale insects are small, sap-sucking pests. The colours can also vary from the most common brown to white, tan, or even orange. They are named for their protective, shell-like coverings, which can be hard or soft depending on the species. They appear as tiny bumps or scales on plant surfaces and often go unnoticed due to their resemblance to plant parts. There are over 8,000 species of scale insects, and they infest a wide range of plants, both indoors and outdoors.
•        Hard Scales (Armored Scales): These have a waxy, shield-like covering and do not produce honeydew. They are typically brown, gray, or black and very small (1-3 mm).
•        Soft Scales: These are larger (up to 6 mm) and have a waxy, sticky coating. They produce honeydew, which can attract ants and lead to sooty mold growth.
•	Scales most often appear as small, brown, and rounded lumps on your plant’s stems, around the leaf joints, and the undersides of leaves. They attach themselves to stems, leaves, or fruit and remain stationary while feeding.
•	They pierce plant tissues with their needle-like mouthparts and suck out the sap, weakening the plant over time.
•	 Scale insects suck the sap out of plants which causes deformed leaves, yellowing leaves, brown marks, and will cause them to eventually fall off if not treated in time.
•	The appearance of sooty mold is another primary sign that indicates scale on plants. This happens when scale insects produce honeydew while feeding on the plants themselves. In turn, this attracts fungal organisms that promote the growth of sooty mold in some (but not all) scales.
•	This type of black-colored fungus disrupts photosynthesis in plants and is a big indicator that scale insects might be feeding on your plant
symptoms:
•	Stunted Growth: By feeding on the plant's sap, scale insects deprive the plant of essential nutrients, leading to slow growth.
•	Yellowing Leaves: Leaves may turn yellow and drop prematurely due to nutrient loss.
•	Reduced Photosynthesis: Heavy infestations block light from reaching the leaves and reduce the plant's ability to photosynthesize.
•	Sooty Mold: Soft scales excrete a sugary substance called honeydew, which promotes the growth of black sooty mold. This mold further reduces photosynthesis and gives plants an unsightly appearance.
causes:
•	They commonly live on the undersides of leaves, stems, branches, and fruit.
•	Scales tend to infest woody plants, while soft scales are often found on tender foliage and fruit.
•	Scale insects rely on living plants to survive, as they feed exclusively on sap.
•	Their immobility and waxy coverings protect them from environmental factors and predators.
•	They thrive in warm, humid conditions but can adapt to various environments, making them challenging to control.
solution:
•	Inspect your plants: First of all, if you suspect your plants have scale insects then you need to first inspect them and check to make sure that’s what they actually are.
•	Prune and dispose of infested branches.
•	Use a cotton swab soaked with rubbing alcohol.
•	Wipe off dead scales using a damp cloth: You can either wash off your plant in a sink or use a soft damp cloth to gently wipe off any dead scales.

Horticultural Oils and Related Products
•	Azamax (azadirachtin): Mix Pure Neem Oil with Coco-Wet and apply every 3-5 days to kill pest eggs indoors and interrupt the reproductive cycle.
Chemical Insecticides
•	Organic pesticides, like insecticidal soap and d-Limonene, can also be used to kill the larvae. However, these products have very little persistence in the environment, so several applications during egg-hatching will be required for effective control.

description:
Root rot is a fungal disease that affects the roots of plants, causing softening and browning of the tissue due to excessive moisture in the soil. 
It is a potentially lethal plant disease that silently attacks the roots of plants, primarily those in wet soil conditions in your containers, without proper drainage. It’s caused by various types of fungus, like fusarium and pythium, and can quickly deplete healthy, white roots, replacing them with soft, brown ones.
symptoms:
•	Yellow leaves: This is usually the first sign most gardeners notice. Don’t ignore yellowing leaves; they might be signaling root rot.
•	Stunted growth: If your plant grows slower or smaller than usual growth it should avoid this disease. 
•	Soft, brown roots: Healthy roots are sturdy and white. If the plant feel mushy and have turned brown, it’s likely due to root decay caused by fungi in overly wet soil.
•	Wilting: Despite sufficient water supply, plants with root rot often appear wilted and droop due to compromised nutrient absorption.
•	Delayed blooming or no flowers: Root rot can affect a plant’s ability to bloom.
solution:
•	Provide good drainage: Whether gardening in containers or out in the yard, ensuring your plants have well-drained soil is crucial. This can prevent water from collecting around the roots of your plants.
•	Clean and disinfect tools: After dealing with a plant suffering from root rot, always sterilize your scissors, shears, and other tools with a bleach solution.
•	Use fresh soil when replanting: If you’ve treated a plant for root rot and removed any damaged roots, use fresh soil with good drainage.
•	Check root health regularly: Keep an eye on the color and firmness of your plant’s roots; healthy roots should be white and firm. Quick detection can save your plant before the disease causes irreparable damage.
•	Fungicide use: This is the most common chemical method to fight off root diseases like rot. It helps curb the spread of dangerous fungi, such as P. cinnamomi and Basidiomycete fungi, known to cause rot in Acacia plants.
•	Carbendazim: This systemic broad-spectrum fungicide can be used to suppress the progression of not only root rot but also other plant diseases.
•	Disinfecting pruning tools: Regular sterilization of gardening tools using a bleach solution helps prevent the transfer and spread of fungal spores between plants.

description:
Leaf spots are very common and generally do not require spraying. Fungal leaf spot disease can be found both indoors on houseplants, and outdoors in the landscape. Leaf spots may result in some defoliation of a plant. An established plant can tolerate almost complete defoliation if it happens late in the season or not every year. Small or newly planted seedlings that become defoliated are more at risk of suffering damage until they become established. 
The disease affects their appearance and health. These diseases manifest as spots, lesions and discoloration on leaves, leading to premature leaf drop, stunted growth, and even plant death if left untreated. 
Spots usually appear in spring as wind and water blow fungal spores onto leaves. As the infection progresses, the spots get larger. Leaves may become so infected that they turn completely brown and drop.
symptoms:
•	Spots and lesions: The most obvious symptom is the presence of spots or lesions on the leaves. These may be small or large, circular or irregular in shape and vary in colour from yellow to orange-red to light brown, brown, or black.
•	Concentric rings: Some leaf spots exhibit concentric rings, which are a hallmark sign of specific fungal diseases.
•	 Fungal bodies: In some cases, you may be able to see fungal bodies on the affected leaves, appearing as fuzzy or powdery structures. These are the fungi's reproductive structures and help confirm the diagnosis.
•	Yellowing and dropping: Severely affected leaves often turn yellow and drop prematurely, leading to a sparse and weakened plant.
•	 Specific symptoms: Different types of leaf spot diseases have specific symptoms Spots form on the upper, lower, or both sides of leaves. For example, anthracnose often causes leaf margins to darken and curl, while cercospora leaf spot typically starts on the lower leaves and progresses upwards.
solution:
•        Remove & Destroy Infected Leaves: Prune and dispose of heavily affected leaves to reduce the source of spores and prevent further spread.
•        Promote air circulation: Improve air circulation around your plants by thinning dense foliage and spacing them adequately. This will help the leaves dry quickly, reducing the risk of fungal growth.
•        Water wisely: Avoid overhead watering, which can spread spores. Instead, water at the base of the plant to keep the foliage dry.
•        Clean up debris: Remove fallen leaves and other plant debris from around your plants, as they can harbour disease-causing organisms.
Home recipes
•	Baking soda: Spraying with a baking soda solution (a tablespoon of baking soda, 2 1/2 tablespoons of vegetable oil, a teaspoon of liquid soap, not detergent, to one gallon of water), or neem oil (do not use when pollinating insects including bees or other beneficial insects are present). Baking soda may burn some plant leaves. 
•	Neem oil is a natural fungicide that effectively controls leaf spot. Spray the affected leaves thoroughly, ensuring good coverage.
•	Spray only a few and then check for a reaction before applying applications every two weeks.
•	Garlic Spray: Garlic can also help combat fungal diseases. Crush garlic cloves and steep them in water overnight. Strain the solution and spray it on the affected plants

Chemical fungicides

•	Apply sulfur sprays or copper-based fungicides weekly at first sign of disease to prevent its spread. These organic fungicides will not kill leaf spot, but prevent the spores from germinating.
•	The products with one of the following active ingredients will enable control, although directions should be checked to ensure suitability for specific plants: triticonazole, myclobutanil. Continue spraying at fortnightly intervals throughout the season.
•	Broad spectrum fungicide: This broad-spectrum bio-fungicide uses a patented strain of Bacillus subtilis that is registered for organic use. Best of all, SERENADE is completely non-toxic to honey bees and beneficial insects.
•	Containing copper and pyrethrins, Bonide® Garden Dust is a safe, one-step control for many insect attacks and fungal problems. For best results, cover both the tops and undersides of leaves with a thin uniform film or dust. Depending on foliage density, 10 oz will cover 625 sq ft. Repeat applications every 7-10 days, as needed.

Nymphs, known as crawlers, hatch from cottony masses of yellow-orange eggs. Crawlers vary in colour from whitish yellow to red until they begin excreting whitish wax.

description:
Thrips are tiny, slender insects and are about 1–2 mm in size, often yellow, brown, or black, and have fringed wings that give them a unique appearance. Thrips are highly mobile and feed by piercing plant tissues and sucking out cell contents. They are common pests in gardens, greenhouses, and indoor plants, causing significant damage to a wide variety of plants.
•	Adult thrips are elongated and narrow with fringed wings, while nymphs (immature stages) are wingless and pale in colour.
•	They are difficult to see with the naked eye, but their damage and presence of tiny black faecal spots are telltale signs.
•	Thrips feed by scraping the plant surface and sucking up the sap, damaging flowers, leaves, and stems.
•	They are fast-moving and can fly or be carried by wind, spreading infestations quickly.
•	Some species act as vectors for plant viruses, compounding the damage.
symptoms:
•	Leaf Discoloration: Feeding causes leaves to develop silvery or pale streaks, spots, or scars.
•	Deformed Growth: Severe infestations can cause leaves and buds to curl, distort, or drop prematurely.
•	Reduced Flower and Fruit Quality: Thrips damage flower petals, causing browning, scarring, or deformation. Fruits may also develop blemishes.
•	Disease Transmission: Thrips are known vectors of viruses, further harming plant health.

solution:
•	Keep plants moist. Plants that are kept too dry are more likely to be damaged by thrips. To limit damage or reduce future damage after other initial control measures are used, keep plants moist and increase humidity.
o	Azadirachtin (neem oil): Mix 1 Tbsp of neem oil per gallon of water and apply it as a soil drench for effective control of soil-borne insect larvae for every 5 to 6 days.
•	Insecticidal soap. Insecticidal soaps, which are considered nontoxic to humans and pets, give good control. Be sure that flowers and growing tips are well covered with the spray. Frequent sprays may be needed until the problem is under control.
•	Alcohol: A combination of 70% rubbing alcohol and water, applied to the body directly, dissolves the exoskeleton and ensures that the thrip succumbs to the elements and dies. This is true also for thrip eggs, and should be reapplied every few days until the infestation is gone.
•	Use superior horticultural oil sprays. Highly refined oils sold as superior or horticultural oils will also control thrips. The oil suffocates the insects. These oils are highly refined and under proper conditions, can be applied to plants in foliage without damage. Follow label directions to avoid damage to some plants that may be sensitive. Superior oils are also considered nontoxic and are less likely to harm beneficial insects. When spraying indoors, protect surfaces that may be damaged by an oil residue.
•	Use sticky traps: Blue and yellow sticky traps are a good way to catch thrips that have left plants and are seeking a new spot to settle down. The trap attracts them, then when they land upon it they are stuck, and cannot spread themselves any further through the home.
•	Spray: For light infestations, thrips can be removed by force, with a spray of water from a pressurised bottle or in the shower. This can physically remove them from the plant without the use of any chemicals or materials.
•	Chemical insecticides: Many insecticides registered for use indoors are available. Sprays containing pyrethrins, a plant-derived insecticide, are effective and more benign than other chemical pesticides. Follow label directions and, if possible, spray out-of-doors or in a garage, weather permitting.

description:
Whiteflies are small, winged insects belonging to the Aleyrodidae family. Despite their name, they are not true flies but are closely related to aphids and mealybugs. They appear as tiny, white, moth-like insects clustered on the undersides of leaves, and they feed by sucking plant sap. Whiteflies are a common pest in gardens, greenhouses, and on indoor plants. 
Whiteflies are most noticeable when disturbed, as they flutter in clouds around the plant. Adults are about 1–2 mm in size, and their nymphs (immature stages) are flat, oval, and translucent, sticking to the undersides of leaves. They have a rapid life cycle, reproducing quickly in warm, humid conditions, making infestations escalate rapidly.
symptoms: Whiteflies damage plants by feeding on their sap, causing yellowing, wilting, and stunted growth. They excrete a sticky substance called honeydew, which promotes the growth of black sooty mold, further reducing photosynthesis. Heavy infestations weaken plants and can transmit plant viruses, leading to severe health declines or crop losses.
causes: Whiteflies thrive on the undersides of leaves, where they lay eggs and avoid predators. They prefer warm, humid climates and are especially problematic in greenhouses. These pests are highly mobile, spreading easily between plants in outdoor gardens and indoor settings.
solution:
•	Spray with water: The first line of defense is to gently spray plants with water to dislodge whitefly eggs and nymphs. Because nymphs don’t move after the initial creeping phase, they will starve and die when removed from their food source.
o	Keep leaves clean: To control honeydew and mold, wipe down affected leaves with a damp cloth or spray with water.
o	horticultural oil: Horticultural oils such as neem oil are also effective. This remedy will kill whiteflies at all life stages and discourage black sooty mold. (Read more on how to use neem oil.)
o	Use yellow sticky traps: For indoor or outdoor infestations, yellow sticky traps can detect and control pests. Whiteflies are attracted to the yellow color and become stuck to the glue-like substance. This remedy also works for other pests including aphids, fungus gnats, and thrips.
•	Alcohol Spray.  Mix 4 ounces of 70% isopropyl alcohol to 12 ounces of water and spray the foliage of plants. Some plants are sensitive to alcohol and foliage can be burned. Test sensitivity by spraying a leaf or two of a plant and wait a day or so to see if there is tolerance. Plants with waxy or hairy leaves tend to be sensitive to alcohol.
Home receipes
•	Garlic spray: Mix 2 teaspoons of cayenne pepper, 4 cloves of garlic and a litre of water. Squeeze the garlic and bring it to a boil along with the cayenne pepper and water. Let it soak overnight in a sealed container. Spray the mixture on the plant with little dish soap. Repeat every other day until all the white fly is gone.
•	Neem oil: Mix 1 teaspoon of Neem oil, 1 tablespoon dish soap, and 1 liter of water and apply that using a spray bottle to the underside of leaves. 
•	Soap spray: Mix 8 drops of dish soap and 1 liter of warm water, pour into a spray bottle, and apply directly to leaves. 
    Chemical insecticides
•	Malathion or Pyrethrins are effective for killing whiteflies. Repeat the spray for every 72 hours (3 days).

description:
Tiny pests are microscopic, very problematic mites can be found in almost any habitat, especially in dry conditions or when humidity is low in surrounding environment. 
Spider mite damage often starts in lower plant growth, expanding into other parts as the mite population increases. A heavy spider mite infestation causes curling, distortion, yellow patches and bronzed patches on the leaves which leads to stippling or yellowing of leaves and fine webbing on the undersides
symptoms:
Pale, yellowed leaves
Leaves look pale or unusually yellow, as if they are in need of fertilizer. This initial symptom is not very helpful to identify the insect, as pale and yellowing of leaves can be caused by different issues on the plants.
Stippling
Leaves have tiny white or yellow spots where mites have been feeding on the plants. This feeding removes chlorophyll, which further gives white patches. Heavy spider mite feeding can result in loss of almost all of the green pigment, but most commonly the pigment is removed in little dots at the feeding area (called stippling).
Bronzing
Some leaf types develop a bronze or brownish cast on them in response to spider mite infection. Depending on the plant type, bronzing may come after or instead of, stippling.
Dusty, gritty feeling leaves
Spider mites themselves are often hard to see, but evidence of their presence can be seen and felt on some leaves. Faecal matter, fine webbing, dead mites and removes the exoskeletons (like skins that have been shed) of young mites collect on leaves. As this matter builds up on leaves, it feels gritty when one’s fingers are rubbed on affected leaves.
Webbing
Fine webbing, which is similar to spider webs, is found on new growth and between leaves. A buildup of webbing is a sign of a severe infestation. Two-spotted spider mite is easiest to see when mites are moving around inside this webbing.
Where will they live and survive?
 Spider mites survive in cracks of the soil and leaf litter in the pots. It’s reproduction is highly favoured by hot and dry conditions. Severe damage occurs in mid-July to September. These are active during cooler weather in spring and fall.
causes: Spider mites survive in cracks of the soil and leaf litter in the pots. It’s reproduction is highly favoured by hot and dry conditions. Severe damage occurs in mid-July to September. These are active during cooler weather in spring and fall.
solution:
To treat infestations, ensuring thorough coverage, including the undersides of leaves for better management.
Knock mites off plants with water 
Spraying with a strong stream of water can dislodge spider mites from plants. Spray water frequently on plants to control future buildups. Use the Bug Blaster to wash plants with a strong stream of water and reduce pest numbers.
Insecticidal soap
Insecticidal soap to be effective, it must cover mites bodies. It may be necessary to move leaves around and upside down to get good coverage. Soap must usually be applied multiple times for effective control. Apply a thorough spray over the entire plant, then again 2–3 days later to cover the new mites that have hatched (eggs are not affected by a soap spray).

Neem oil. Apply as for soap to cover mites’ bodies. To protect pollinators, avoid using neem oil when plants are blooming;

When temperatures exceed 80°F, both soap and neem oil can further damage plants. Test a small area of the plant before applying these products during high temperatures.
Horticultural oil spray 
Apply horticultural oils to the affected plants during the early stages of infestation. Highly refined oils sold as superior or horticultural oils are also very effective in controlling spider mites. The oil suffocates the mites. Unlike dormant oils, these oils are highly refined and under proper conditions, can be applied to plant foliage without damage. Superior oils are considered nontoxic and are less likely to kill beneficial insects. 
Mix Pure Neem Oil with Coco-Wet and apply every 3-5 days to kill pest eggs indoors and interrupt the reproductive cycle. Make sure to spray all plant parts, including the undersides of leaves. Do not apply when temperatures exceed 90˚F and wait at least six hours before turning lights on.
Chemical insecticides or miticides 
A very safe product made from the seeds of a tropical tree is called Neem. It is commercially available under the name Margosan-O. Other chemical controls include malathion, bifenthrin, cyfluthrin, and kelthane. Many pesticides are very harmful to bees and fish when used improperly.
Nuke Em, a relatively new organic insecticide containing food-grade ingredients, works fast and kills most indoor gardening pests at the egg, larvae, or adult stage. Best of all, it does this without leaving a residue on the leaves that can impact flavor.

BotaniGard ES is another highly effective biological insecticide that you can consider using. It contains Beauveria bassiana, an entomopathogenic fungus that attacks a long list of troublesome crop pests – even resistant strains! Weekly applications can prevent insect population explosions and provide protection equal to or better than conventional chemical pesticides.
If populations are high, use a least-toxic, short-lived pesticide (Take Down Spray, Doktor Doom Foggers) to reduce infestations

description:
Scale insects are small, sap-sucking pests. The colours can also vary from the most common brown to white, tan, or even orange. They are named for their protective, shell-like coverings, which can be hard or soft depending on the species. They appear as tiny bumps or scales on plant surfaces and often go unnoticed due to their resemblance to plant parts. There are over 8,000 species of scale insects, and they infest a wide range of plants, both indoors and outdoors.
•        Hard Scales (Armored Scales): These have a waxy, shield-like covering and do not produce honeydew. They are typically brown, gray, or black and very small (1-3 mm).
•        Soft Scales: These are larger (up to 6 mm) and have a waxy, sticky coating. They produce honeydew, which can attract ants and lead to sooty mold growth.
•	Scales most often appear as small, brown, and rounded lumps on your plant’s stems, around the leaf joints, and the undersides of leaves. They attach themselves to stems, leaves, or fruit and remain stationary while feeding.
•	They pierce plant tissues with their needle-like mouthparts and suck out the sap, weakening the plant over time.
•	 Scale insects suck the sap out of plants which causes deformed leaves, yellowing leaves, brown marks, and will cause them to eventually fall off if not treated in time.
•	The appearance of sooty mold is another primary sign that indicates scale on plants. This happens when scale insects produce honeydew while feeding on the plants themselves. In turn, this attracts fungal organisms that promote the growth of sooty mold in some (but not all) scales.
•	This type of black-colored fungus disrupts photosynthesis in plants and is a big indicator that scale insects might be feeding on your plant
symptoms:
•	Stunted Growth: By feeding on the plant's sap, scale insects deprive the plant of essential nutrients, leading to slow growth.
•	Yellowing Leaves: Leaves may turn yellow and drop prematurely due to nutrient loss.
•	Reduced Photosynthesis: Heavy infestations block light from reaching the leaves and reduce the plant's ability to photosynthesize.
•	Sooty Mold: Soft scales excrete a sugary substance called honeydew, which promotes the growth of black sooty mold. This mold further reduces photosynthesis and gives plants an unsightly appearance.
causes:
•	They commonly live on the undersides of leaves, stems, branches, and fruit.
•	Scales tend to infest woody plants, while soft scales are often found on tender foliage and fruit.
•	Scale insects rely on living plants to survive, as they feed exclusively on sap.
•	Their immobility and waxy coverings protect them from environmental factors and predators.
•	They thrive in warm, humid conditions but can adapt to various environments, making them challenging to control.
solution:
•	Inspect your plants: First of all, if you suspect your plants have scale insects then you need to first inspect them and check to make sure that’s what they actually are.
•	Prune and dispose of infested branches.
•	Use a cotton swab soaked with rubbing alcohol.
•	Wipe off dead scales using a damp cloth: You can either wash off your plant in a sink or use a soft damp cloth to gently wipe off any dead scales.

Horticultural Oils and Related Products
•	Azamax (azadirachtin): Mix Pure Neem Oil with Coco-Wet and apply every 3-5 days to kill pest eggs indoors and interrupt the reproductive cycle.
Chemical Insecticides
•	Organic pesticides, like insecticidal soap and d-Limonene, can also be used to kill the larvae. However, these products have very little persistence in the environment, so several applications during egg-hatching will be required for effective control.

description:
Root rot is a fungal disease that affects the roots of plants, causing softening and browning of the tissue due to excessive moisture in the soil. 
It is a potentially lethal plant disease that silently attacks the roots of plants, primarily those in wet soil conditions in your containers, without proper drainage. It’s caused by various types of fungus, like fusarium and pythium, and can quickly deplete healthy, white roots, replacing them with soft, brown ones.
symptoms:
•	Yellow leaves: This is usually the first sign most gardeners notice. Don’t ignore yellowing leaves; they might be signaling root rot.
•	Stunted growth: If your plant grows slower or smaller than usual growth it should avoid this disease. 
•	Soft, brown roots: Healthy roots are sturdy and white. If the plant feel mushy and have turned brown, it’s likely due to root decay caused by fungi in overly wet soil.
•	Wilting: Despite sufficient water supply, plants with root rot often appear wilted and droop due to compromised nutrient absorption.
•	Delayed blooming or no flowers: Root rot can affect a plant’s ability to bloom.
solution:
•	Provide good drainage: Whether gardening in containers or out in the yard, ensuring your plants have well-drained soil is crucial. This can prevent water from collecting around the roots of your plants.
•	Clean and disinfect tools: After dealing with a plant suffering from root rot, always sterilize your scissors, shears, and other tools with a bleach solution.
•	Use fresh soil when replanting: If you’ve treated a plant for root rot and removed any damaged roots, use fresh soil with good drainage.
•	Check root health regularly: Keep an eye on the color and firmness of your plant’s roots; healthy roots should be white and firm. Quick detection can save your plant before the disease causes irreparable damage.
•	Fungicide use: This is the most common chemical method to fight off root diseases like rot. It helps curb the spread of dangerous fungi, such as P. cinnamomi and Basidiomycete fungi, known to cause rot in Acacia plants.
•	Carbendazim: This systemic broad-spectrum fungicide can be used to suppress the progression of not only root rot but also other plant diseases.
•	Disinfecting pruning tools: Regular sterilization of gardening tools using a bleach solution helps prevent the transfer and spread of fungal spores between plants.

description:
Leaf spots are very common and generally do not require spraying. Fungal leaf spot disease can be found both indoors on houseplants, and outdoors in the landscape. Leaf spots may result in some defoliation of a plant. An established plant can tolerate almost complete defoliation if it happens late in the season or not every year. Small or newly planted seedlings that become defoliated are more at risk of suffering damage until they become established. 
The disease affects their appearance and health. These diseases manifest as spots, lesions and discoloration on leaves, leading to premature leaf drop, stunted growth, and even plant death if left untreated. 
Spots usually appear in spring as wind and water blow fungal spores onto leaves. As the infection progresses, the spots get larger. Leaves may become so infected that they turn completely brown and drop.
symptoms:
•	Spots and lesions: The most obvious symptom is the presence of spots or lesions on the leaves. These may be small or large, circular or irregular in shape and vary in colour from yellow to orange-red to light brown, brown, or black.
•	Concentric rings: Some leaf spots exhibit concentric rings, which are a hallmark sign of specific fungal diseases.
•	 Fungal bodies: In some cases, you may be able to see fungal bodies on the affected leaves, appearing as fuzzy or powdery structures. These are the fungi's reproductive structures and help confirm the diagnosis.
•	Yellowing and dropping: Severely affected leaves often turn yellow and drop prematurely, leading to a sparse and weakened plant.
•	 Specific symptoms: Different types of leaf spot diseases have specific symptoms Spots form on the upper, lower, or both sides of leaves. For example, anthracnose often causes leaf margins to darken and curl, while cercospora leaf spot typically starts on the lower leaves and progresses upwards.
solution:
•        Remove & Destroy Infected Leaves: Prune and dispose of heavily affected leaves to reduce the source of spores and prevent further spread.
•        Promote air circulation: Improve air circulation around your plants by thinning dense foliage and spacing them adequately. This will help the leaves dry quickly, reducing the risk of fungal growth.
•        Water wisely: Avoid overhead watering, which can spread spores. Instead, water at the base of the plant to keep the foliage dry.
•        Clean up debris: Remove fallen leaves and other plant debris from around your plants, as they can harbour disease-causing organisms.
Home recipes
•	Baking soda: Spraying with a baking soda solution (a tablespoon of baking soda, 2 1/2 tablespoons of vegetable oil, a teaspoon of liquid soap, not detergent, to one gallon of water), or neem oil (do not use when pollinating insects including bees or other beneficial insects are present). Baking soda may burn some plant leaves. 
•	Neem oil is a natural fungicide that effectively controls leaf spot. Spray the affected leaves thoroughly, ensuring good coverage.
•	Spray only a few and then check for a reaction before applying applications every two weeks.
•	Garlic Spray: Garlic can also help combat fungal diseases. Crush garlic cloves and steep them in water overnight. Strain the solution and spray it on the affected plants

Chemical fungicides

•	Apply sulfur sprays or copper-based fungicides weekly at first sign of disease to prevent its spread. These organic fungicides will not kill leaf spot, but prevent the spores from germinating.
•	The products with one of the following active ingredients will enable control, although directions should be checked to ensure suitability for specific plants: triticonazole, myclobutanil. Continue spraying at fortnightly intervals throughout the season.
•	Broad spectrum fungicide: This broad-spectrum bio-fungicide uses a patented strain of Bacillus subtilis that is registered for organic use. Best of all, SERENADE is completely non-toxic to honey bees and beneficial insects.
•	Containing copper and pyrethrins, Bonide® Garden Dust is a safe, one-step control for many insect attacks and fungal problems. For best results, cover both the tops and undersides of leaves with a thin uniform film or dust. Depending on foliage density, 10 oz will cover 625 sq ft. Repeat applications every 7-10 days, as needed.

description:
White waxy secretions were found on mealy bugs that cover their bodies. The waxy-white, slow-moving, wingless females typically feed in large, sticky colonies. Nymphs, known as crawlers, hatch from cottony masses of yellow-orange eggs. Crawlers vary in colour from whitish yellow to red until they begin excreting whitish wax. 
In warmer climates, mealybugs are serious pests on many garden and ornamental plants. In this area, a wide variety of indoor and tropical plants, summered outdoors or maintained in greenhouses can be attacked, as they can attack many outdoor woody trees and shrubs, perennials and summer annuals.
Some mealybug species can hide and survive as nymphs and eggs. Reappearance of them in the spring often come from introduction of mealybug infested plants, with young nymphs from the infested plant colonizing nearby plants.
symptoms:
The leaves on plants are covered with black speckles and spots. At first, you suspect some type of fungus, but, upon closer inspection, you find tufts of cottony material and segmented waxy bugs. 
Mealybugs weaken plants by sucking juices from plant stems and leaves. Damaged plants show wilting, curling and discoloration of leaves. Leaves may drop prematurely and flowering may be delayed. Twigs and small branches may die back. Mealybugs excrete a sweet substance known as honeydew, which often develops into black sooty mold. 
Overwatering and over-fertilizing can cause mealybug infestations because the insects prefer plants with high nitrogen levels and soft growth. Properly watering and feeding plants not only reduces the possibility of mealybug infestation but is also essential for preventing plant diseases.
solution:
Manual removal of mealybugs
Depending on host plant size and scope of infestation, remove mealybugs with alcohol-dipped cotton swabs or physically knock them off plants with a forceful water spray and repeat as necessary. 
Treatment with isopropyl alcohol
Prune out light infestations or dab insects dipped in rubbing alcohol. On small infestations on plants, a 70 % or less solution of isopropyl (rubbing) alcohol in water may be dabbed directly on mealybugs with a cotton swab to kill them or remove them. 
If infestations are extensive, a 10-25 % solution of isopropyl alcohol can be applied with a spray bottle. Repeat this procedure every week until the infestation is reduced.
Homemade spray recipes
•	Vegetable oil: Mix 1 tablespoon mild dish soap or 1 tablespoon vegetable oil & 1 cup water. Mix 1/4 cup rubbing alcohol with 1 cup of water. You can either dab it on the mealybugs with a cotton swab or spray it on.
•	Paraffin oil: Paraffin oil coats the mealybugs with a thin film of oil and suffocates them, which leads to death of mealybugs. Paraffin oil is extremely effective but, paraffin products must never be used in direct sunlight, otherwise the plant can suffer burns.

•	Methylated spirit: Spray a one-percent solution (10ml of spirit for 1 litre of water) on the infested plant. The solution will dissolve the waxy layer that surrounds and protects the insects, making the pests vulnerable. The methylated spirit penetrates the insects and they perish.

•	Soapy spray: The waxy layer of mealybugs is also destroyed by soft soap. Use liquid soap for cleaning for leaf surface and dilute with water, as a spray against mealybugs.
•	Garlic broth: Chop 50 g of fresh garlic (Allium sativum) and pour one and a half litres of boiling water over it. This mixture should soak for about half an hour and then strained. After it is cooled, the garlic extract can be sprayed onto the affected plants.

•	Don’t overwater or overfertilize: Do not overwater or over fertilize your plants both indoors and outdoors. Mealybugs are attracted to plants with high nitrogen levels and soft growth.
Chemical insecticides 
•	Nonchemical methods usually provide sufficient control for outdoor plantings in gardens and landscapes. Home and garden insecticides are not very effective for mealybugs, especially on larger plants. 
•	Mixing of 2 per cent methyl parathion dust or 1.5% chlorpyriphos dust @ 250 gm per plant.
•	Spray 0.04% monocrotophos or 0.06% dimethoate if nymphs have already ascended the plant.
•	Neem kernel extracts and a commercially produced neem extract-based product (Rakshak) induces mild ovicidal action and appreciable nymphal and adults mortality.

symptoms:
Powdery mildew fungi produce structures that are inserted into plant cells, allowing them to extract nutrients required for development and spore production.
This results in a general loss in the host’s growth and health, with noticeable symptoms. This includes abnormal growth, such as leaf curling, twisting and yellowing may be observed before the fungus’s white symptoms are visible.
The white symptoms appear as circular white, powdery spots, hence why it’s called powdery mildew. 
•	Splotches on the surface of leaves: These are often the most obvious signs of powdery mildew. However, the disease starts on the undersides of leaves and also appears on the stems, flower buds and even fruit.
•	Withering and yellow leaves: This happens because powdery mildew can absorb important nutrients from the plant.
•	Fallen leaves: If the leaf surface covered with powdery mildew, photosynthesis is impaired and the infected leaves will drop from the plant prematurely.
solution:
•	Removal of infected portions of plants or cut back the portions of the plants with visible powdery mildew.
•	Remove individual leaves from the affected plants: Do not compost them because this can allow the spores to spread.
•	Wash your hands and clean your clippers with alcohol wipes: This will further prevent the spread of the disease.
•	Use a thick layer of mulch or organic compost to cover the soil after you have raked and cleaned it well. Mulch will prevent the disease spores from splashing back up onto the leaves.
•	Water in the morning, so plants have a chance to dry during the day. Drip irrigation and soaker hoses will help keep the foliage dry.
•	Use a slow-release, organic fertilizer on crops and avoid excess nitrogen. Soft, leafy, new growth is most susceptible.

Homemade recipes
•	Milk Spray: Milk sprays, made with 40% milk and 60% water, are an effective home remedy for use on a wide range of plants. For best results, spray plant leaves as a preventative measure every 10-14 days.

•	Baking Soda: Baking soda is one of the best home remedies for treating powdery mildew. For this method, 1ix 1 tablespoon baking soda and ½ teaspoon liquid soap in 1 gallon of water. Transfer it into a spray bottle and spray the tops and underside of leaves and any other affected areas.
•	Although this works best as a preventative measure, it’s also known to be effective on existing powdery mildew infections as well.
•	Wash Foliage: Wash foliage occasionally to disrupt the daily spore-releasing cycle. Neem oil and PM Wash, used on a 7-day schedule, will prevent a fungal attack on plants grown indoors.

Chemical fungicides

•	Sulphur or Copper-based fungicide: Apply sulphur or copper-based fungicides to prevent infection of susceptible plants. For best results, apply early or at the first sign of disease. Spray all plant parts thoroughly and repeat at 7–10 day intervals up to the day of harvest.

•	Potassium bicarbonate: Mix 1-2 Tbsp/ gallon of water and apply to all exposed surfaces of the plant. Monterey® BI-CARB is a similar product containing micro-encapsulated potassium bicarbonate as the active ingredient. Mix 4 teaspoons in 2 gallons of water to thoroughly cover foliage.

•	Broad-Spectrum Fungicide: This broad-spectrum bio-fungicide uses a patented strain of Bacillus subtilis that is approved for organic gardening. Best of all, it’s safe to use — you can treat and pick crops on the same day!

•	Sulfur Burner for Indoor Plants: Indoor growers may want to consider using a Sulfur Burner/ Vaporizer which turns sulfur prills into fine dust and changes the pH of leaf surfaces.
Fungal spores and mold can’t get established on this plant coating. As an added benefit, studies have shown that this dust will eliminate spider mites.

description:
Aphids are small, pear-shaped, soft-bodied insects, colour ranges from green, black, red, yellow, brown or gray. They are present in cluster densely on tender new growth and the undersides of leaves for sucking plant juices. Plants often can withstand some aphid feeding with no adverse effect, but badly infested plants develop distorted growth and leaves may turn yellow or drop off.
Many species of aphids feed on home garden plants; these insects range in color from pale green, pink, or black to red or yellow. Adult aphids are generally wingless, but winged adults will appear when overcrowded. Immature aphids (nymphs) closely resemble adults.
Both adults and nymphs feed on a wide variety of both outdoor plants and houseplants. In small numbers aphids do little damage, but they are able to reproduce rapidly and can quickly become a more serious problem. Also, as they feed, aphids secrete a sweet fluid called honeydew that can attract ants; sooty black fungus may grow on coated leaves.
symptoms: Clusters of small, soft-bodied insects were observed undersides of leaves, along stems, and around buds and flowers with the naked eye. Aphids can cause stunted growth with curled or distorted leaves and can weaken the plant They secrete a sweet, sticky substance called honeydew as they feed, which can coat leaves and attract other pests like ants. This honeydew can also cause a fungal growth called sooty mold. These can cause yellowed or curled leaves, stunted growth and reduced yields.
solution:
Clusters of small, soft-bodied insects were observed undersides of leaves, along stems, and around buds and flowers with the naked eye. Aphids can cause stunted growth with curled or distorted leaves and can weaken the plant
They secrete a sweet, sticky substance called honeydew as they feed, which can coat leaves and attract other pests like ants. This honeydew can also cause a fungal growth called sooty mold. These can cause yellowed or curled leaves, stunted growth and reduced yields. 
How to control/manage them ?
•	Hose them off: A strong blast of water from a hose can dislodge aphids from plants. Be sure to direct the stream of water underneath leaves and into crevices where aphids may be hiding.

•	Use yellow sticky traps: Yellow sticky traps are a safe and easy way to get rid of aphids. The bright yellow colour attracts aphids, who then get stuck to the sticky surface. These yellow traps resemble a healthy plant leaf and so attract aphids to the sticky trap and work really well. This effective insect glue can last for up to 3 months as well.
•	Diatomaceous earth: Consider applying 100% organic diatomaceous earth for long-lasting protection. Made up of tiny fossilized aquatic organisms, that look like broken glass under the microscope, DE kills by scoring an aphid’s outer layer as it crawls over the fine powder.

•	Remove infested plants: In some cases, the best solution is to remove infested plants from your garden. This will help prevent the spread of aphids to other plants. Again, the help of professionals may be best here to make sure the job is done properly.

•	Pick aphid eggs and aphids off by hands: Aphids don’t move quickly, so its easy to just pick them off. Wear rubber gloves and wipe them off into bucket of soap water. 
Homemade spray recipes
•	Vegetable oil: mix 1 tablespoon mild dish soap or 1 tablespoon vegetable oil & 1 cup water. Mix 1/4 cup rubbing alcohol with 1 cup of water. 
•	Garlic spray: Mix a few drops of pure castile soap with water in a spray bottle and shake well. Spray the solution onto your plants, focusing on the areas where aphids are present. The soap will suffocate the aphids and cause them to die off. Repeat this process every few days until the aphids are gone. 

•	Essential oils: Essential oils can also be added to homemade solutions. For example, peppermint, clove, rosemary, thyme, and hot pepper are essential oils that can be helpful pest deterrents.

Insecticidal soaps: Safer® Soap will work fast on heavy infestations. A short-lived natural pesticide, it works by damaging the outer layer of soft-bodied insect pests, causing dehydration and death within hours. Apply 2.5 oz/gallon of water when insects are present, repeat every 7-10 days as needed.
Use Horticultural Oils and Products: Bon-Neem is a unique blend of potassium soaps derived from Indian Neem tree seed and other natural sources. It’s specially formulated as a ready-to-use spray that kills most insect pests on contact.
Horticultural oils should be applied early in the season or late in the fall to destroy overwintering eggs. Neem oil sprays are another great option that you can use.

Chemical insecticides 
BotaniGard ES is a highly effective biological insecticide containing Beauveria bassiana, an entomopathogenic fungus that attacks a long-list of troublesome crop pests – even resistant strains! Weekly applications can prevent insect population explosions and provide protection equal to or better than conventional chemical pesticides.

Fast-acting botanical insecticides should be used as a last resort. Derived from plants which have insecticidal properties, these natural pesticides have fewer harmful side effects than synthetic chemicals and break down more quickly in the environment.

description:
Thrips are tiny, slender insects and are about 1–2 mm in size, often yellow, brown, or black, and have fringed wings that give them a unique appearance. Thrips are highly mobile and feed by piercing plant tissues and sucking out cell contents. They are common pests in gardens, greenhouses, and indoor plants, causing significant damage to a wide variety of plants.
•	Adult thrips are elongated and narrow with fringed wings, while nymphs (immature stages) are wingless and pale in colour.
•	They are difficult to see with the naked eye, but their damage and presence of tiny black faecal spots are telltale signs.
•	Thrips feed by scraping the plant surface and sucking up the sap, damaging flowers, leaves, and stems.
•	They are fast-moving and can fly or be carried by wind, spreading infestations quickly.
•	Some species act as vectors for plant viruses, compounding the damage.
symptoms:
•	Leaf Discoloration: Feeding causes leaves to develop silvery or pale streaks, spots, or scars.
•	Deformed Growth: Severe infestations can cause leaves and buds to curl, distort, or drop prematurely.
•	Reduced Flower and Fruit Quality: Thrips damage flower petals, causing browning, scarring, or deformation. Fruits may also develop blemishes.
•	Disease Transmission: Thrips are known vectors of viruses, further harming plant health.
causes:
•	Leaf Discoloration: Feeding causes leaves to develop silvery or pale streaks, spots, or scars.
•	Deformed Growth: Severe infestations can cause leaves and buds to curl, distort, or drop prematurely.
•	Reduced Flower and Fruit Quality: Thrips damage flower petals, causing browning, scarring, or deformation. Fruits may also develop blemishes.
•	Disease Transmission: Thrips are known vectors of viruses, further harming plant health.
solution:
•	Keep plants moist. Plants that are kept too dry are more likely to be damaged by thrips. To limit damage or reduce future damage after other initial control measures are used, keep plants moist and increase humidity.
o	Azadirachtin (neem oil): Mix 1 Tbsp of neem oil per gallon of water and apply it as a soil drench for effective control of soil-borne insect larvae for every 5 to 6 days.
•	Insecticidal soap. Insecticidal soaps, which are considered nontoxic to humans and pets, give good control. Be sure that flowers and growing tips are well covered with the spray. Frequent sprays may be needed until the problem is under control.
•	Alcohol: A combination of 70% rubbing alcohol and water, applied to the body directly, dissolves the exoskeleton and ensures that the thrip succumbs to the elements and dies. This is true also for thrip eggs, and should be reapplied every few days until the infestation is gone.
•	Use superior horticultural oil sprays. Highly refined oils sold as superior or horticultural oils will also control thrips. The oil suffocates the insects. These oils are highly refined and under proper conditions, can be applied to plants in foliage without damage. Follow label directions to avoid damage to some plants that may be sensitive. Superior oils are also considered nontoxic and are less likely to harm beneficial insects. When spraying indoors, protect surfaces that may be damaged by an oil residue.
•	Use sticky traps: Blue and yellow sticky traps are a good way to catch thrips that have left plants and are seeking a new spot to settle down. The trap attracts them, then when they land upon it they are stuck, and cannot spread themselves any further through the home.
•	Spray: For light infestations, thrips can be removed by force, with a spray of water from a pressurised bottle or in the shower. This can physically remove them from the plant without the use of any chemicals or materials.
•	Chemical insecticides: Many insecticides registered for use indoors are available. Sprays containing pyrethrins, a plant-derived insecticide, are effective and more benign than other chemical pesticides. Follow label directions and, if possible, spray out-of-doors or in a garage, weather permitting.

description:
Whiteflies are small, winged insects belonging to the Aleyrodidae family. Despite their name, they are not true flies but are closely related to aphids and mealybugs. They appear as tiny, white, moth-like insects clustered on the undersides of leaves, and they feed by sucking plant sap. Whiteflies are a common pest in gardens, greenhouses, and on indoor plants. 
Whiteflies are most noticeable when disturbed, as they flutter in clouds around the plant. Adults are about 1–2 mm in size, and their nymphs (immature stages) are flat, oval, and translucent, sticking to the undersides of leaves. They have a rapid life cycle, reproducing quickly in warm, humid conditions, making infestations escalate rapidly.
symptoms: Whiteflies damage plants by feeding on their sap, causing yellowing, wilting, and stunted growth. They excrete a sticky substance called honeydew, which promotes the growth of black sooty mold, further reducing photosynthesis. Heavy infestations weaken plants and can transmit plant viruses, leading to severe health declines or crop losses.
causes: Whiteflies thrive on the undersides of leaves, where they lay eggs and avoid predators. They prefer warm, humid climates and are especially problematic in greenhouses. These pests are highly mobile, spreading easily between plants in outdoor gardens and indoor settings.
solution:
•	Spray with water: The first line of defense is to gently spray plants with water to dislodge whitefly eggs and nymphs. Because nymphs don’t move after the initial creeping phase, they will starve and die when removed from their food source.
o	Keep leaves clean: To control honeydew and mold, wipe down affected leaves with a damp cloth or spray with water.
o	horticultural oil: Horticultural oils such as neem oil are also effective. This remedy will kill whiteflies at all life stages and discourage black sooty mold. (Read more on how to use neem oil.)
o	Use yellow sticky traps: For indoor or outdoor infestations, yellow sticky traps can detect and control pests. Whiteflies are attracted to the yellow color and become stuck to the glue-like substance. This remedy also works for other pests including aphids, fungus gnats, and thrips.
•	Alcohol Spray.  Mix 4 ounces of 70% isopropyl alcohol to 12 ounces of water and spray the foliage of plants. Some plants are sensitive to alcohol and foliage can be burned. Test sensitivity by spraying a leaf or two of a plant and wait a day or so to see if there is tolerance. Plants with waxy or hairy leaves tend to be sensitive to alcohol.
Home receipes
•	Garlic spray: Mix 2 teaspoons of cayenne pepper, 4 cloves of garlic and a litre of water. Squeeze the garlic and bring it to a boil along with the cayenne pepper and water. Let it soak overnight in a sealed container. Spray the mixture on the plant with little dish soap. Repeat every other day until all the white fly is gone.
•	Neem oil: Mix 1 teaspoon of Neem oil, 1 tablespoon dish soap, and 1 liter of water and apply that using a spray bottle to the underside of leaves. 
•	Soap spray: Mix 8 drops of dish soap and 1 liter of warm water, pour into a spray bottle, and apply directly to leaves. 
    Chemical insecticides
•	Malathion or Pyrethrins are effective for killing whiteflies. Repeat the spray for every 72 hours (3 days).

description:
Tiny pests are microscopic, very problematic mites can be found in almost any habitat, especially in dry conditions or when humidity is low in surrounding environment. 
Spider mite damage often starts in lower plant growth, expanding into other parts as the mite population increases. A heavy spider mite infestation causes curling, distortion, yellow patches and bronzed patches on the leaves which leads to stippling or yellowing of leaves and fine webbing on the undersides
symptoms:
Pale, yellowed leaves
Leaves look pale or unusually yellow, as if they are in need of fertilizer. This initial symptom is not very helpful to identify the insect, as pale and yellowing of leaves can be caused by different issues on the plants.
Stippling
Leaves have tiny white or yellow spots where mites have been feeding on the plants. This feeding removes chlorophyll, which further gives white patches. Heavy spider mite feeding can result in loss of almost all of the green pigment, but most commonly the pigment is removed in little dots at the feeding area (called stippling).
Bronzing
Some leaf types develop a bronze or brownish cast on them in response to spider mite infection. Depending on the plant type, bronzing may come after or instead of, stippling.
Dusty, gritty feeling leaves
Spider mites themselves are often hard to see, but evidence of their presence can be seen and felt on some leaves. Faecal matter, fine webbing, dead mites and removes the exoskeletons (like skins that have been shed) of young mites collect on leaves. As this matter builds up on leaves, it feels gritty when one’s fingers are rubbed on affected leaves.
Webbing
Fine webbing, which is similar to spider webs, is found on new growth and between leaves. A buildup of webbing is a sign of a severe infestation. Two-spotted spider mite is easiest to see when mites are moving around inside this webbing.
Where will they live and survive?
 Spider mites survive in cracks of the soil and leaf litter in the pots. It’s reproduction is highly favoured by hot and dry conditions. Severe damage occurs in mid-July to September. These are active during cooler weather in spring and fall.
causes: Spider mites survive in cracks of the soil and leaf litter in the pots. It’s reproduction is highly favoured by hot and dry conditions. Severe damage occurs in mid-July to September. These are active during cooler weather in spring and fall.
solution:
To treat infestations, ensuring thorough coverage, including the undersides of leaves for better management.
Knock mites off plants with water 
Spraying with a strong stream of water can dislodge spider mites from plants. Spray water frequently on plants to control future buildups. Use the Bug Blaster to wash plants with a strong stream of water and reduce pest numbers.
Insecticidal soap
Insecticidal soap to be effective, it must cover mites bodies. It may be necessary to move leaves around and upside down to get good coverage. Soap must usually be applied multiple times for effective control. Apply a thorough spray over the entire plant, then again 2–3 days later to cover the new mites that have hatched (eggs are not affected by a soap spray).

Neem oil. Apply as for soap to cover mites’ bodies. To protect pollinators, avoid using neem oil when plants are blooming;

When temperatures exceed 80°F, both soap and neem oil can further damage plants. Test a small area of the plant before applying these products during high temperatures.
Horticultural oil spray 
Apply horticultural oils to the affected plants during the early stages of infestation. Highly refined oils sold as superior or horticultural oils are also very effective in controlling spider mites. The oil suffocates the mites. Unlike dormant oils, these oils are highly refined and under proper conditions, can be applied to plant foliage without damage. Superior oils are considered nontoxic and are less likely to kill beneficial insects. 
Mix Pure Neem Oil with Coco-Wet and apply every 3-5 days to kill pest eggs indoors and interrupt the reproductive cycle. Make sure to spray all plant parts, including the undersides of leaves. Do not apply when temperatures exceed 90˚F and wait at least six hours before turning lights on.
Chemical insecticides or miticides 
A very safe product made from the seeds of a tropical tree is called Neem. It is commercially available under the name Margosan-O. Other chemical controls include malathion, bifenthrin, cyfluthrin, and kelthane. Many pesticides are very harmful to bees and fish when used improperly.
Nuke Em, a relatively new organic insecticide containing food-grade ingredients, works fast and kills most indoor gardening pests at the egg, larvae, or adult stage. Best of all, it does this without leaving a residue on the leaves that can impact flavor.

BotaniGard ES is another highly effective biological insecticide that you can consider using. It contains Beauveria bassiana, an entomopathogenic fungus that attacks a long list of troublesome crop pests – even resistant strains! Weekly applications can prevent insect population explosions and provide protection equal to or better than conventional chemical pesticides.
If populations are high, use a least-toxic, short-lived pesticide (Take Down Spray, Doktor Doom Foggers) to reduce infestations

description:
Scale insects are small, sap-sucking pests. The colours can also vary from the most common brown to white, tan, or even orange. They are named for their protective, shell-like coverings, which can be hard or soft depending on the species. They appear as tiny bumps or scales on plant surfaces and often go unnoticed due to their resemblance to plant parts. There are over 8,000 species of scale insects, and they infest a wide range of plants, both indoors and outdoors.
•        Hard Scales (Armored Scales): These have a waxy, shield-like covering and do not produce honeydew. They are typically brown, gray, or black and very small (1-3 mm).
•        Soft Scales: These are larger (up to 6 mm) and have a waxy, sticky coating. They produce honeydew, which can attract ants and lead to sooty mold growth.
•	Scales most often appear as small, brown, and rounded lumps on your plant’s stems, around the leaf joints, and the undersides of leaves. They attach themselves to stems, leaves, or fruit and remain stationary while feeding.
•	They pierce plant tissues with their needle-like mouthparts and suck out the sap, weakening the plant over time.
•	 Scale insects suck the sap out of plants which causes deformed leaves, yellowing leaves, brown marks, and will cause them to eventually fall off if not treated in time.
•	The appearance of sooty mold is another primary sign that indicates scale on plants. This happens when scale insects produce honeydew while feeding on the plants themselves. In turn, this attracts fungal organisms that promote the growth of sooty mold in some (but not all) scales.
•	This type of black-colored fungus disrupts photosynthesis in plants and is a big indicator that scale insects might be feeding on your plant
symptoms:
•	Stunted Growth: By feeding on the plant's sap, scale insects deprive the plant of essential nutrients, leading to slow growth.
•	Yellowing Leaves: Leaves may turn yellow and drop prematurely due to nutrient loss.
•	Reduced Photosynthesis: Heavy infestations block light from reaching the leaves and reduce the plant's ability to photosynthesize.
•	Sooty Mold: Soft scales excrete a sugary substance called honeydew, which promotes the growth of black sooty mold. This mold further reduces photosynthesis and gives plants an unsightly appearance.
causes:
•	They commonly live on the undersides of leaves, stems, branches, and fruit.
•	Scales tend to infest woody plants, while soft scales are often found on tender foliage and fruit.
•	Scale insects rely on living plants to survive, as they feed exclusively on sap.
•	Their immobility and waxy coverings protect them from environmental factors and predators.
•	They thrive in warm, humid conditions but can adapt to various environments, making them challenging to control.
solution:
•	Inspect your plants: First of all, if you suspect your plants have scale insects then you need to first inspect them and check to make sure that’s what they actually are.
•	Prune and dispose of infested branches.
•	Use a cotton swab soaked with rubbing alcohol.
•	Wipe off dead scales using a damp cloth: You can either wash off your plant in a sink or use a soft damp cloth to gently wipe off any dead scales.

Horticultural Oils and Related Products
•	Azamax (azadirachtin): Mix Pure Neem Oil with Coco-Wet and apply every 3-5 days to kill pest eggs indoors and interrupt the reproductive cycle.
Chemical Insecticides
•	Organic pesticides, like insecticidal soap and d-Limonene, can also be used to kill the larvae. However, these products have very little persistence in the environment, so several applications during egg-hatching will be required for effective control.

description:
Root rot is a fungal disease that affects the roots of plants, causing softening and browning of the tissue due to excessive moisture in the soil. 
It is a potentially lethal plant disease that silently attacks the roots of plants, primarily those in wet soil conditions in your containers, without proper drainage. It’s caused by various types of fungus, like fusarium and pythium, and can quickly deplete healthy, white roots, replacing them with soft, brown ones.
symptoms:
•	Yellow leaves: This is usually the first sign most gardeners notice. Don’t ignore yellowing leaves; they might be signaling root rot.
•	Stunted growth: If your plant grows slower or smaller than usual growth it should avoid this disease. 
•	Soft, brown roots: Healthy roots are sturdy and white. If the plant feel mushy and have turned brown, it’s likely due to root decay caused by fungi in overly wet soil.
•	Wilting: Despite sufficient water supply, plants with root rot often appear wilted and droop due to compromised nutrient absorption.
•	Delayed blooming or no flowers: Root rot can affect a plant’s ability to bloom.
solution:
•	Provide good drainage: Whether gardening in containers or out in the yard, ensuring your plants have well-drained soil is crucial. This can prevent water from collecting around the roots of your plants.
•	Clean and disinfect tools: After dealing with a plant suffering from root rot, always sterilize your scissors, shears, and other tools with a bleach solution.
•	Use fresh soil when replanting: If you’ve treated a plant for root rot and removed any damaged roots, use fresh soil with good drainage.
•	Check root health regularly: Keep an eye on the color and firmness of your plant’s roots; healthy roots should be white and firm. Quick detection can save your plant before the disease causes irreparable damage.
•	Fungicide use: This is the most common chemical method to fight off root diseases like rot. It helps curb the spread of dangerous fungi, such as P. cinnamomi and Basidiomycete fungi, known to cause rot in Acacia plants.
•	Carbendazim: This systemic broad-spectrum fungicide can be used to suppress the progression of not only root rot but also other plant diseases.
•	Disinfecting pruning tools: Regular sterilization of gardening tools using a bleach solution helps prevent the transfer and spread of fungal spores between plants.

description:
Leaf spots are very common and generally do not require spraying. Fungal leaf spot disease can be found both indoors on houseplants, and outdoors in the landscape. Leaf spots may result in some defoliation of a plant. An established plant can tolerate almost complete defoliation if it happens late in the season or not every year. Small or newly planted seedlings that become defoliated are more at risk of suffering damage until they become established. 
The disease affects their appearance and health. These diseases manifest as spots, lesions and discoloration on leaves, leading to premature leaf drop, stunted growth, and even plant death if left untreated. 
Spots usually appear in spring as wind and water blow fungal spores onto leaves. As the infection progresses, the spots get larger. Leaves may become so infected that they turn completely brown and drop.
symptoms:
•	Spots and lesions: The most obvious symptom is the presence of spots or lesions on the leaves. These may be small or large, circular or irregular in shape and vary in colour from yellow to orange-red to light brown, brown, or black.
•	Concentric rings: Some leaf spots exhibit concentric rings, which are a hallmark sign of specific fungal diseases.
•	 Fungal bodies: In some cases, you may be able to see fungal bodies on the affected leaves, appearing as fuzzy or powdery structures. These are the fungi's reproductive structures and help confirm the diagnosis.
•	Yellowing and dropping: Severely affected leaves often turn yellow and drop prematurely, leading to a sparse and weakened plant.
•	 Specific symptoms: Different types of leaf spot diseases have specific symptoms Spots form on the upper, lower, or both sides of leaves. For example, anthracnose often causes leaf margins to darken and curl, while cercospora leaf spot typically starts on the lower leaves and progresses upwards.
solution:
•        Remove & Destroy Infected Leaves: Prune and dispose of heavily affected leaves to reduce the source of spores and prevent further spread.
•        Promote air circulation: Improve air circulation around your plants by thinning dense foliage and spacing them adequately. This will help the leaves dry quickly, reducing the risk of fungal growth.
•        Water wisely: Avoid overhead watering, which can spread spores. Instead, water at the base of the plant to keep the foliage dry.
•        Clean up debris: Remove fallen leaves and other plant debris from around your plants, as they can harbour disease-causing organisms.
Home recipes
•	Baking soda: Spraying with a baking soda solution (a tablespoon of baking soda, 2 1/2 tablespoons of vegetable oil, a teaspoon of liquid soap, not detergent, to one gallon of water), or neem oil (do not use when pollinating insects including bees or other beneficial insects are present). Baking soda may burn some plant leaves. 
•	Neem oil is a natural fungicide that effectively controls leaf spot. Spray the affected leaves thoroughly, ensuring good coverage.
•	Spray only a few and then check for a reaction before applying applications every two weeks.
•	Garlic Spray: Garlic can also help combat fungal diseases. Crush garlic cloves and steep them in water overnight. Strain the solution and spray it on the affected plants

Chemical fungicides

•	Apply sulfur sprays or copper-based fungicides weekly at first sign of disease to prevent its spread. These organic fungicides will not kill leaf spot, but prevent the spores from germinating.
•	The products with one of the following active ingredients will enable control, although directions should be checked to ensure suitability for specific plants: triticonazole, myclobutanil. Continue spraying at fortnightly intervals throughout the season.
•	Broad spectrum fungicide: This broad-spectrum bio-fungicide uses a patented strain of Bacillus subtilis that is registered for organic use. Best of all, SERENADE is completely non-toxic to honey bees and beneficial insects.
•	Containing copper and pyrethrins, Bonide® Garden Dust is a safe, one-step control for many insect attacks and fungal problems. For best results, cover both the tops and undersides of leaves with a thin uniform film or dust. Depending on foliage density, 10 oz will cover 625 sq ft. Repeat applications every 7-10 days, as needed.

description:
White waxy secretions were found on mealy bugs that cover their bodies. The waxy-white, slow-moving, wingless females typically feed in large, sticky colonies. Nymphs, known as crawlers, hatch from cottony masses of yellow-orange eggs. Crawlers vary in colour from whitish yellow to red until they begin excreting whitish wax. 
In warmer climates, mealybugs are serious pests on many garden and ornamental plants. In this area, a wide variety of indoor and tropical plants, summered outdoors or maintained in greenhouses can be attacked, as they can attack many outdoor woody trees and shrubs, perennials and summer annuals.
Some mealybug species can hide and survive as nymphs and eggs. Reappearance of them in the spring often come from introduction of mealybug infested plants, with young nymphs from the infested plant colonizing nearby plants.
symptoms:
The leaves on plants are covered with black speckles and spots. At first, you suspect some type of fungus, but, upon closer inspection, you find tufts of cottony material and segmented waxy bugs. 
Mealybugs weaken plants by sucking juices from plant stems and leaves. Damaged plants show wilting, curling and discoloration of leaves. Leaves may drop prematurely and flowering may be delayed. Twigs and small branches may die back. Mealybugs excrete a sweet substance known as honeydew, which often develops into black sooty mold. 
Overwatering and over-fertilizing can cause mealybug infestations because the insects prefer plants with high nitrogen levels and soft growth. Properly watering and feeding plants not only reduces the possibility of mealybug infestation but is also essential for preventing plant diseases.
solution:
Manual removal of mealybugs
Depending on host plant size and scope of infestation, remove mealybugs with alcohol-dipped cotton swabs or physically knock them off plants with a forceful water spray and repeat as necessary. 
Treatment with isopropyl alcohol
Prune out light infestations or dab insects dipped in rubbing alcohol. On small infestations on plants, a 70 % or less solution of isopropyl (rubbing) alcohol in water may be dabbed directly on mealybugs with a cotton swab to kill them or remove them. 
If infestations are extensive, a 10-25 % solution of isopropyl alcohol can be applied with a spray bottle. Repeat this procedure every week until the infestation is reduced.
Homemade spray recipes
•	Vegetable oil: Mix 1 tablespoon mild dish soap or 1 tablespoon vegetable oil & 1 cup water. Mix 1/4 cup rubbing alcohol with 1 cup of water. You can either dab it on the mealybugs with a cotton swab or spray it on.
•	Paraffin oil: Paraffin oil coats the mealybugs with a thin film of oil and suffocates them, which leads to death of mealybugs. Paraffin oil is extremely effective but, paraffin products must never be used in direct sunlight, otherwise the plant can suffer burns.

•	Methylated spirit: Spray a one-percent solution (10ml of spirit for 1 litre of water) on the infested plant. The solution will dissolve the waxy layer that surrounds and protects the insects, making the pests vulnerable. The methylated spirit penetrates the insects and they perish.

•	Soapy spray: The waxy layer of mealybugs is also destroyed by soft soap. Use liquid soap for cleaning for leaf surface and dilute with water, as a spray against mealybugs.
•	Garlic broth: Chop 50 g of fresh garlic (Allium sativum) and pour one and a half litres of boiling water over it. This mixture should soak for about half an hour and then strained. After it is cooled, the garlic extract can be sprayed onto the affected plants.

•	Don’t overwater or overfertilize: Do not overwater or over fertilize your plants both indoors and outdoors. Mealybugs are attracted to plants with high nitrogen levels and soft growth.
Chemical insecticides 
•	Nonchemical methods usually provide sufficient control for outdoor plantings in gardens and landscapes. Home and garden insecticides are not very effective for mealybugs, especially on larger plants. 
•	Mixing of 2 per cent methyl parathion dust or 1.5% chlorpyriphos dust @ 250 gm per plant.
•	Spray 0.04% monocrotophos or 0.06% dimethoate if nymphs have already ascended the plant.
•	Neem kernel extracts and a commercially produced neem extract-based product (Rakshak) induces mild ovicidal action and appreciable nymphal and adults mortality.

symptoms:
Powdery mildew fungi produce structures that are inserted into plant cells, allowing them to extract nutrients required for development and spore production.
This results in a general loss in the host’s growth and health, with noticeable symptoms. This includes abnormal growth, such as leaf curling, twisting and yellowing may be observed before the fungus’s white symptoms are visible.
The white symptoms appear as circular white, powdery spots, hence why it’s called powdery mildew. 
•	Splotches on the surface of leaves: These are often the most obvious signs of powdery mildew. However, the disease starts on the undersides of leaves and also appears on the stems, flower buds and even fruit.
•	Withering and yellow leaves: This happens because powdery mildew can absorb important nutrients from the plant.
•	Fallen leaves: If the leaf surface covered with powdery mildew, photosynthesis is impaired and the infected leaves will drop from the plant prematurely.
solution:
•	Removal of infected portions of plants or cut back the portions of the plants with visible powdery mildew.
•	Remove individual leaves from the affected plants: Do not compost them because this can allow the spores to spread.
•	Wash your hands and clean your clippers with alcohol wipes: This will further prevent the spread of the disease.
•	Use a thick layer of mulch or organic compost to cover the soil after you have raked and cleaned it well. Mulch will prevent the disease spores from splashing back up onto the leaves.
•	Water in the morning, so plants have a chance to dry during the day. Drip irrigation and soaker hoses will help keep the foliage dry.
•	Use a slow-release, organic fertilizer on crops and avoid excess nitrogen. Soft, leafy, new growth is most susceptible.

Homemade recipes
•	Milk Spray: Milk sprays, made with 40% milk and 60% water, are an effective home remedy for use on a wide range of plants. For best results, spray plant leaves as a preventative measure every 10-14 days.

•	Baking Soda: Baking soda is one of the best home remedies for treating powdery mildew. For this method, 1ix 1 tablespoon baking soda and ½ teaspoon liquid soap in 1 gallon of water. Transfer it into a spray bottle and spray the tops and underside of leaves and any other affected areas.
•	Although this works best as a preventative measure, it’s also known to be effective on existing powdery mildew infections as well.
•	Wash Foliage: Wash foliage occasionally to disrupt the daily spore-releasing cycle. Neem oil and PM Wash, used on a 7-day schedule, will prevent a fungal attack on plants grown indoors.

Chemical fungicides

•	Sulphur or Copper-based fungicide: Apply sulphur or copper-based fungicides to prevent infection of susceptible plants. For best results, apply early or at the first sign of disease. Spray all plant parts thoroughly and repeat at 7–10 day intervals up to the day of harvest.

•	Potassium bicarbonate: Mix 1-2 Tbsp/ gallon of water and apply to all exposed surfaces of the plant. Monterey® BI-CARB is a similar product containing micro-encapsulated potassium bicarbonate as the active ingredient. Mix 4 teaspoons in 2 gallons of water to thoroughly cover foliage.

•	Broad-Spectrum Fungicide: This broad-spectrum bio-fungicide uses a patented strain of Bacillus subtilis that is approved for organic gardening. Best of all, it’s safe to use — you can treat and pick crops on the same day!

•	Sulfur Burner for Indoor Plants: Indoor growers may want to consider using a Sulfur Burner/ Vaporizer which turns sulfur prills into fine dust and changes the pH of leaf surfaces.
Fungal spores and mold can’t get established on this plant coating. As an added benefit, studies have shown that this dust will eliminate spider mites.
